title: Human Dignity and Justice
subtitle: An ethical framework for speaking about Palestinian lives and every human life — Written for sincere seekers asking whether Islam is true.
summary: For sincere seekers asking whether Islam is true: A source-aware library should treat human dignity as a starting point. This draft offers an Islamic ethical framework for discussing suffering and injustice without excusing harm, spreading hatred, or making claims beyond the evidence.

sections.title: For a Seeker Asking Whether Islam Is True
sections.body:
This article is written for a sincere seeker asking whether Islam is true. It is not only a neutral comparison or an interfaith description.

A method article is useful only if it leads beyond comparison: the reader should use its distinctions to investigate Islam's claims about God, revelation, accountability, and the Quran.

Where historians or scholars disagree, the article identifies the main alternatives before drawing its Islamic implication.

Read the labels carefully: an explicit Quranic or Prophetic text, an established Sunni teaching, a classical or modern scholarly interpretation, a historical reconstruction, and the author's inference are different kinds of claim. Disputed questions should be identified as disputed rather than hidden.

sections.title: In Plain Words
sections.body:
Human dignity means that a person is not merely a statistic, a slogan, or a representative of a group. Every person has moral worth. A discussion of Palestine that forgets this fails before it begins.

Dignity does not cancel difficult questions about history, law, security, or responsibility. It changes how those questions are asked: with truthful language, refusal of collective blame, and care for civilians and vulnerable people.

sections.title: An Islamic Ethical Starting Point
sections.body:
The Qur'an describes the children of Adam as honoured, and Islamic ethics repeatedly joins justice with truthfulness and mercy. Muslims understand these teachings as obligations toward human beings, not permissions to value only people from their own group.

Applying a principle requires humility. A religious text can guide moral reasoning, but it does not remove the need to establish facts, distinguish intentional harm from rumour, and recognise the limits of one's knowledge.

sections.title: Practical Standards for Speech and Action
sections.body:
Do not assign guilt to an entire people for the actions of leaders, institutions, or armed groups. Do not circulate graphic images or casualty figures without checking the source, date, and context. Do not use another community's pain as a rhetorical tool.

A fair response to suffering can include prayer, charitable support through accountable organisations, careful learning, and principled advocacy. It should never include dehumanisation, false witness, or celebration of harm.

sections.title: Applying the Principle to a Hard Claim
sections.body:
If an armed group attacks civilians, justice requires naming the act and identifying the responsible actors. It does not justify treating every member of the surrounding people, religion, or ethnicity as guilty. If a government uses force, the same rule applies: distinguish the government's decision, the conduct of particular units, and the civilians who may be harmed or may oppose it.

This distinction is not moral weakness. It makes accountability more precise, protects vulnerable people from collective blame, and leaves room to condemn real wrongdoing without turning grief into hatred.

sections.title: What This Means for a Seeker
sections.body:
This article is one part of a larger truth-seeking case. Its subject should not be treated as an isolated proof or as a reason to stop at comparison. The Islamic claim is that the Quran restores clear guidance about the one God and calls human beings to respond to Him with faith, worship, repentance, and moral responsibility.

A method article is useful only if it leads beyond comparison: the reader should use its distinctions to investigate Islam's claims about God, revelation, accountability, and the Quran.

If you are asking whether Islam is true, take a direct next step: read the Quran itself in a reliable translation, revisit the primary sources linked here, and write down the strongest objection that remains. Ask God sincerely for guidance and take that question to a trustworthy, knowledgeable Muslim. The aim is not to win an interfaith argument or to caricature alternatives, but to investigate Islam honestly and then respond to its claim.

furtherReading.title: The Qur'an: A New Translation
furtherReading.author: M. A. S. Abdel Haleem
furtherReading.note: A widely used modern English translation; consult Arabic and recognised tafsir for detailed legal or theological interpretation.

furtherReading.title: The Ethics of War and Peace in Islam
furtherReading.author: Majid Khadduri
furtherReading.note: A foundational academic study of Islamic legal and ethical traditions; later scholarship should be consulted for critique and development.

faq.question: If I am asking whether Islam is true, what should I do next?
faq.answer: Begin with the Quran in a reliable translation and the primary sources linked in this article. Ask God sincerely for guidance, note the strongest question that remains, and discuss it with a trustworthy, knowledgeable Muslim. A method article is useful only if it leads beyond comparison: the reader should use its distinctions to investigate Islam's claims about God, revelation, accountability, and the Quran.
